sections.brief: The UN mediator's mission from his appointment (20 May 1948) to his assassination (17 September 1948): the two truces, the 28 June Rhodes suggestions (union with Transjordan, Jerusalem to the Arab side, Negev/Galilee, unrestricted return) and the 16 September report (Negev to the Arabs, Galilee to Israel, Jerusalem under UN control, return 'at the earliest possible date', a conciliation commission, merger of Arab Palestine with Transjordan), and why both sides rejected the first plan. Present the minor dispute over which UN body appointed him. Tell the killing only briefly (Lehi, Sérot killed with him) and link to [scene:mil_s01|the absorption of the undergrounds] for the dissolution and amnesty; end by pointing to how the report fed Resolution 194 and Marshall's endorsement in tr_s02. Figures: a comparison of the June suggestions and the September report (territory, Jerusalem, refugees, Transjordan); a timeline May–September 1948.

Truman's decisions from June 1948 to May 1950 in strict date order: the Displaced Persons Act, Marshall's 21 September endorsement of the Bernadotte plan and Clifford's objection, the 24 October pledge, the 29 November Negev assurance, the $100 million Export-Import Bank loan and de jure recognition (31 January 1949), the secret 28 May 1949 note threatening a 'revision' of policy, Israel's June rejection, and the Tripartite Declaration of May 1950. Present both readings fairly ('donors bought policy' vs 'money played no role') and show what the dated record supports: timing clustered around the election, then pressure that was threatened but not enforced. Draw from cia_s02 only its 1948 material (the CIA and State warnings overruled, de jure recognition) and link forward for Angleton and the later liaison. Embed money_1948:Dollar Flows:0 and discuss the $100M loan against the $0.1M Feinberg figure; figure: timeline June 1948–May 1950.

Abraham Feinberg as a person and a channel, 1945–1958: the hosiery fortune, the Sonneborn link, the $100,000 raised with Ed Kaufmann for the whistle-stop tour, Judis's account of Truman backing off over territory and refugees (tell the decision itself briefly and link to tr_s02 rather than repeat its chronology), Feinberg's own words on 'campaign money', the 1952 order to register under FARA for Israel Speaks and its closure (from fis_s05), and Ben-Gurion's 1958 'call Abe' nuclear fundraising role, stated as Avner Cohen's account and linked forward. Keep the claim at its documented size: one historian's account of one decision, not proof of a general purchase. Embed money_1948:Dollar Flows:1 and discuss why the smallest figure is the one tied to a decision; figure: a money chain (donors → Feinberg/Kaufmann → campaign train → Truman's retreat on pressure → refugees and territory question left unpressed).

How return was barred and the border hardened, June 1948–1956: the cabinet decision of 16 June 1948 that there could be no return during the war, the occupation of abandoned houses, Morris's finding of no top-level expulsion order alongside commanders' authority (via Hertzberg), then the 'infiltration' years: Morris's estimate that 90% or more of crossings were economic and social, 2,700–5,000 infiltrators killed (mostly unarmed), the shoot-on-sight policy, Qibya (October 1953, 69 killed), the activist–moderate split between Ben-Gurion and Sharett, and from the Israeli side the 1955 fedayeen organized by Egyptian intelligence. Present the dispute over what infiltration was from both sides with equal care. Link forward to [scene:mg_s01|Kafr Qasim, 1956] and the Suez war; keep 1955–56 brief. Figure: timeline 1948–1956; key figures (2,700–5,000; 90%; 69; 45 houses).

Who would govern Arab Palestine, September 1948–July 1951: the Arab League's July and September 1948 decisions, the All-Palestine Government proclaimed in Gaza (22 September) under Ahmad Hilmi, the Palestinian National Council under Hajj Amin al-Husayni (30 September), recognitions and Abdullah's refusal; the rival Amman congress and the Jericho Congress (1 December 1948); Egypt's administration of Gaza (from egi_src_s02, 1948–1956 only); the Arab Legion, the renaming of the kingdom (April 1949), the April 1950 elections, the 24 April 1950 union resolution and its 'two banks' language (ijr_src_s05), Britain's cabinet decision of 25 April 1950, and Abdullah's assassination (20 July 1951). Give Palestinian political agency its full weight, including Shlaim's verdict that the Gaza government was a 'phantom' created by Arab states; present the recognition dispute (Britain only; Britain and Pakistan; Britain, Iraq and Pakistan) without resolving it, and note Jordan's denial of Jewish access to the Old City's holy sites. Figure: power structure of Arab Palestine in 1949 (Arab League, Egypt/Gaza and APG, Jordan/West Bank); timeline September 1948–July 1951.

The Palestinian Arabs who stayed inside Israel and the regime imposed on them: the population figures (156,000 non-Jews at the end of 1948, 167,100 in 1950), the first Knesset vote and the Democratic List of Nazareth's 2 seats, then the military government from October 1948: the 1945 Defence (Emergency) Regulations and Regulation 125, the 1949 Security Zones regulations, permits without legal basis until January 1950, conviction statistics, the Rattner Commission (1956). Present the dispute over its purpose (security vs control of movement and land). Draw from mg_s01 the 1949–1956 regime; tell Kafr Qasim (29 October 1956) briefly with its documented figures and the 'black flag' doctrine, and carry the story to abolition (1 December 1966) and the Toledano letter only in a closing paragraph that links forward. Figures: process flow of how a permit regime worked (regulation → closed area → permit → conviction); key figures (156,000; 1 in 3 held permits in 1958; 2,714 of 2,888 convicted in 1955).

The legal chain that turned flight into state ownership, July 1948–1953: Custodian of Abandoned Property (15 July 1948), the December 1948 Emergency Regulations (note the 2 vs 12 December date discrepancy), the Absentees' Property Law of 14 March 1950 and its text, the 'present absentees' (about 200,000 by 2001), the Conciliation Commission's April 1949 request to suspend the law, the Development Authority (1950), sales and transfers to the JNF, and the Land Acquisition Law of 1953. Attribute the BADIL and Adalah figures (2.4 million dunams transferred; 92% state-held by 1951; 1.2–1.3 million dunams from 349 localities) as theirs, set them beside the scholarly sources, and say plainly what totals the record does not settle. Mention military rule's role in keeping internal refugees from their land and link to rd6_military_government rather than repeating it. Figures: process flow (Custodian 1948 → Absentees' Property Law 1950 → Development Authority → JNF / state land → 1953 validation); comparison of 'absentee' in plain meaning vs in law.

The week of 9–11 December 1948 and the machinery it did and did not create: no rights treaty system before 1948 (the League mandates, the Red Cross and de Reynier at Deir Yassin), the Genocide Convention, the Universal Declaration (48–0–8) and Article 13(2), Resolution 194 (tell only that it passed and link to rr_s01 for its text), UNRWA (created December 1949, operating May 1950; relief, not return), Article 1D of the 1951 Refugee Convention, and the ICC's absence until 2002. Explain plainly why Palestinian refugees ended up outside the UNHCR system and what that meant in the 1950s; state Israel's position that neither UDHR 13(2) nor 194 creates a binding right of return for descendants. Embed money_1948:Land & People:2 and discuss the ~700,000 and ~711,000 figures. Figure: timeline December 1948–1951 (the rights instruments and UNRWA).

Resolution 194 (11 December 1948) read as a whole: the vote (35–15–8), the Conciliation Commission (France, Turkey, the United States), Jerusalem under 'effective United Nations control' and free access (paragraphs 7–9), the call to negotiate a final settlement (paragraph 5), and paragraph 11 in full, including its mandate for 'repatriation, resettlement and economic and social rehabilitation'. Present the two readings with their strongest evidence: Israel's (conditional on peace, a recommendation, demographic consequences) and the Palestinian (a right, reaffirmed annually, tied to Israel's UN admission), and record that Arab states first rejected it. Then the numbers dispute: 520,000–530,000 (Israel's official figure), 711,000–726,000 (UN), Eytan's private 'close to 800,000', 810,000 (British) and 900,000–1 million (Arab officials), and the village counts (369, 418, 531) with their definitions. Figures: comparison of the refugee estimates by source; a comparison of what paragraph 11 says and how each side reads it.

The Rhodes armistices of 1949, from the primary texts: Bunche's January talks; Egypt (24 February: Faluja withdrawal, El Auja demilitarized, Gaza–Rafah frozen, the 'not a political or territorial boundary' clause, the Mixed Armistice Commission); Lebanon (23 March, from ilb_s02, with the 100,000–110,000 refugees who went there); Jordan (3 April: the Special Committee on holy places, Mount Scopus and the Latrun road; the Wadi Ara transfer and the villagers' guaranteed rights); Syria (20 July); Iraq's refusal to sign (covered by the Jordan agreement, per Bunche; link to rd6_exodus for Iraq's 1948 laws) and Saudi Arabia's non-signature and the Arab League boycott (isa_src_s02). Explain what an armistice is and is not, and quote Bunche's 21 July letter on 'non-aggression' and the end of the mediator's role. Embed prestate_funding:Overview:0 to set the 56% partition share against the Foreign Ministry's 'about 78%' inside the Green Line, and year_ledger:Part 6:0 for the 1949 row; figures: timeline of the four signatures; comparison of the four agreements (date, signatories, key clause, commission).

The state's first institutions and the constitution that was deferred, May 1948–June 1950: the Declaration's promise of a constitution by 1 October 1948, the January 1949 election, the Constituent Assembly convening on 14 February 1949 and renaming itself the Knesset, Ben-Gurion's reasons for opposing a written constitution and the religious parties' demand on personal status, and the Harari Resolution of 13 June 1950 (chapters as Basic Laws). Draw from ilgov_s01, ilgov_s02 and ilgov_s04 only what applies to 1948–1950s (no constitution, coalition formation, president and prime minister) and link forward for the Basic Laws to the present and the 2023 crisis. Figure: power structure of the state's institutions in 1949 (Knesset, government, president, courts).

Syria in 1949 and the frontier it left: Husni al-Za'im's coup (30 March 1949) and the debate over US contacts (from me_s08), his offer of peace, a summit and resettlement of 250,000–300,000 refugees, Ben-Gurion's refusal and why, Za'im's overthrow and execution (August 1949), the 20 July armistice and its demilitarized zones, and the 1950s DMZ clashes (Dayan's 1953–54 'someone must keep the area alive'; Dayan's later 'at least 80 percent' claim, presented as contested). Present the 'Syria rejected every chance' claim and the counter-record fairly, including Syrian fire on farmers and fishermen. Tell the water war of 1964–67 and the later coups (Egypt 1952, Iran 1953, Iraq 1958) only in a sentence each, linking forward. Map: syria_line.

The Lausanne conference (27 April–12 September 1949): the Conciliation Commission created by Resolution 194, shuttle diplomacy because Arab delegations refused direct talks, the 12 May Protocol on the 1947 map, the Gaza proposal, Israel's 3 August offer of 100,000 (to a maximum of 250,000 Arabs) 'only as an integral part of a general and final peace settlement', the Arab demand for return first, the blocked committee on refugee-owned orange groves, and the withdrawal of the offer. Weave in Truman's 28 May note and its unenforced threat (link to tr_s02 rather than retell), and the Commission's April 1949 request to suspend the absentee law (link to ap_s01). Present both sequences (peace first vs return first) fairly and say what the record does not settle about whether either could have moved. Figure: comparison of the Israeli and Arab positions (sequence, territory, refugees, Jerusalem).

Israel's admission to the UN and the Jerusalem question, March 1949–January 1950: recognition by Turkey (March 1949, the first Muslim-majority state, from tk_s03; link forward for Trident and the 1990s alliance), the Ad Hoc Political Committee's questioning of Israel on Jerusalem, refugees and the Bernadotte investigation (6 May 1949), Resolution 273 (11 May 1949, 37–12–9) and its text recalling Resolutions 181 and 194, the Vatican's campaign to condition admission on refugee return and the holy sites (from vat_s01; Ben-Gurion's 'historical reckoning'), Resolution 303 (9 December 1949), Ben-Gurion's response, the Knesset's move (26 December) and the 23 January 1950 declaration of Jerusalem as capital (60–2). State that Eban's specific assurances are not in the documents fetched and must be attributed to the scene that cites them (rr_s01). Figure: timeline March 1949–January 1950.

Where the refugees went and how host states treated them, 1948–1950s, set against the older Latin American diaspora (Bethlehem families from the 1870s, the 'Turcos', Chile's Club Palestino of 1920, El Salvador's 1921 'pernicious races' decree, Saca and Bukele). For 1948: Jordan, the West Bank, Gaza, Lebanon and Syria; UNRWA registration from 1950; Lebanon's non-naturalization and its sectarian reasoning (ilb_s03); Jordan's 1954 nationality law and the Arab League's line on preserving return (sq_s20), each told only for the 1948–1950s and linked forward. Present both readings of host-state policy (protecting a claim of return vs keeping refugees in limbo as a political tool). Link to [scene:hma_src_s02|Palestinian political origins] for how the camps became the base of later movements. Figure: comparison of the two migrations (date, origin, destination, legal status).

The Jews of the Arab world after 1948, country by country: Iraq's July 1948 law making Zionism a crime, the hanging of Shafiq Ades (23 September 1948), the March 1950 denaturalization law, the disputed 1950–51 bombings (both positions, as the source requires) and Operation Ezra and Nehemiah; Yemen and Operation Magic Carpet (June 1949–September 1950, the walk to Aden); Morocco (the Oujda and Jérada riots of 7–8 June 1948; Operation Yachin only in a forward sentence); Egypt (75,000 in 1948, the 1948 bombings in Cairo's Jewish quarter, the 1956 expulsions briefly); Libya. Use me_s07's 800,000–900,000 range and Mendes's 'nearly one million', and present the three readings of why they left (Arab violence, Zionist agitation, push and pull) with Mendes's judgment. Name real antisemitism plainly where the record shows it, and never generalize about Arabs or Muslims. Map: me_layers; figure: key figures by country (Iraq, Yemen, Libya, Egypt, Morocco).

The mass immigration of 1948–1952 and what it did to the new state: 203,000 in the first year, 684,201 by the end of 1951, the State Archives table (738,891 by the end of 1952: 377,251 from Muslim countries and 307,082 from Communist states, with the country figures), Cyprus detainees and DP-camp survivors first, then whole communities; immigrant camps (112,015 in May 1950), the ma'abarot (113 camps, 250,000 people by May 1952), the 1951 peak and the 1952–54 slowdown (51,463), and the austerity regime from coupons to the 1959 abolition. Note the discrepancies in the Iraqi and Yemeni totals across sources. Set up the hierarchy that mz_s02 documents without retelling it. Figures: key figures; a comparison of the origins of immigrants (Muslim countries vs Communist states vs West).

The Yemenite Children Affair, 1948–1954, with its afterlife to 2021: the transit camps and the European-born Labor leadership, the families' account of infants taken and declared dead without bodies or death certificates, the three inquiries from 1967 (most died of disease), Israel Hayom's documents suggesting possible state involvement, and the February 2021 decision (NIS 162 million, about 1,050 families, 'regret' without apology). Present the dispute between the inquiries' findings and the families' allegations without resolving it beyond the record. Link back to rd6_exodus for the Yemeni airlift. Figure: timeline 1948–2021.

Who belongs: the Law of Return (5 July 1950; note the 3 vs 5 July dispute) and the Nationality Law (in force 14 July 1952), from their texts: section 1's right of every Jew, the visa exclusions, the 1954 amendment, the 'by return' vs 'by residence' routes and the residence test (registered on 1 March 1952) that former Palestinian citizens had to meet, and the retroactive repeal of Palestinian citizenship. Present the strongest case for the law in its own terms (Ben-Gurion: a right 'inherent in every Jew' that 'preceded the State'; the refuge argument after the Holocaust) and the strongest critique (Kassim: discrimination against Palestinians who lived on the land; statelessness), plus the Jewish internal debates. Mention the 1970 'who is a Jew' amendment only in a forward sentence. Figure: comparison of the two routes to nationality (who qualifies, conditions, effect).

The American organization after statehood, 1949–1963: AZEC renamed the American Zionist Council in 1949; from s11 only the founding of the American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs by Isaiah Kenen in 1953–54 and why (fear of foreign-agent registration), renamed AIPAC in 1959; the November 1962 Justice Department order alleging over $5 million from the Jewish Agency over eight years; the withdrawn demand and the 1963 restructuring. The two scenes date AIPAC's emergence differently (1953–54/1959 vs 1963): present both and say what each refers to. Keep the 1953 Iran coup out except as a one-line link forward. Figure: timeline 1943–1963 of the organization's names.

How the new state was paid for, 1949–1953: the US aid series from the CRS table (100.0 in 1949, nothing in 1950, 35.1 in 1951, 86.4 in 1952, rising to 85.4 in 1958; economic only, with the military-aid start dated 1959 in the table and 1962 in iaa_s01; present both), Israel Bonds (conceived 1950, launched the next spring, $52 million in the first year, 35% of the development budget within six years), and the German reparations: Sharett's $1.5 billion claim (500,000 × $3,000), the 61–50 Knesset vote of 9 January 1952 and the protests Begin led, the Luxembourg signing (10 September 1952), the payment mechanics and their share of imports. Present the two valuations ($845 million vs 3.5 billion marks plus 450 million) and the moral dispute over 'blood money' fairly. Embed money_1948:Dollar Flows:0 (the $100M loan) and aid_arms:Overview:2 (economic aid only until the 1960s); figures: money chain for reparations (Germany → goods and oil → Israel's imports → development → who bore the cost and who objected); key figures.

How the flight was explained, 1948–1988, as the first of the chapter's accounting sections: Deir Yassin reported within days and documented by the Red Cross, the 'Arab radio told them to leave' explanation and its official adoption, the Einstein–Arendt letter of 4 December 1948, Walid Khalidi (1959) and Erskine Childers (1961) on the broadcast monitoring records, and Morris (1988) from the Israeli archives (attack, expulsion and fear; local evacuation orders; no general order). Present the strongest form of each side's case and what mainstream scholarship no longer defends, and state what remains disputed (intent and planning; link to the Plan Dalet scene). Figure: timeline 1948–1988 from story to record.

How support for Israel was argued to Americans in 1948 and how that changed: refuge (some 250,000 Jewish DPs), Christian restorationist belief and democracy; the national-security establishment's opposite view (State, the Joint Chiefs, the Defense Secretary, the CIA); the use of the Mufti's real wartime collaboration in anti-Arab framing; the later, separately documented anti-Islam network; and 'strategic asset' as a post-1967 argument formalized under Reagan in 1981. Keep each later development to a forward sentence. Map: warnings_1947.

Did money buy the politicians before 1948? Decompose the question into its four claims and score each: organized pressure (documented in detail), money changing one decision (Feinberg/Kaufmann, documented once; link to s07f2), systematic payments to Congress (cannot be established either way because the Federal Corrupt Practices Act of 1925 required little disclosure until FECA in 1971), and other drivers that point the same way without money. State plainly that absence of records proves neither side. Embed money_1948:Dollar Flows:1 and money_1948:The Machine:1; figure: comparison of the four claims (claim, evidence, verdict).

Who paid for it all, 1899–1949: Keren Hayesod's $20.1 million (1921–29) by country, the UJA's wartime and postwar campaigns ($124M+ 1939–45, $100M 1946, ~$110M 1947, $150M in 1948 from over a million donors in 4,950 communities) and the 1948 split ($74.7M UPA, $64.9M JDC, $10.4M USNA), the arms money as ranges, and the CPI method for today's dollars. Stress that much of the 1948 total fed Holocaust survivors in Europe and that no audited grand total exists. Embed global_funding:Overview:0, global_funding:By Country:0, global_funding:Where It Went:0 and global_funding:The Arms Bill:0, and discuss their numbers; figure: money chain (donors → federations/UJA → UPA/JDC/USNA → immigration, settlement, defense → who bore the cost).

The operating budgets and Britain's bill, 1922–1948: the Jewish Agency's £720,000 budget of 1939 with £80,000 for 'security service (defense)', the 1944–46 growth to a $56 million request, Kofer HaYishuv (1938), the June 1948 advertisement calling the UJA 'the official American agency for aid to Haganah', and Britain's costs (£P1.9M civil budget 1922–23 to £P3.2M 1934–35; £1.5M garrison 1923–24; about £100 million for forces in 1945–47, some 100,000 troops; about 750 killed). Say plainly that the Haganah's total budget is not documented. Embed global_funding:Budgets & Britain:0, global_funding:Defense Money:0 and global_funding:Gaps & Method:0; figure: key figures.

The network of the American build-up, 1897–1948, tier by tier with each tie's documented type: apex (Jewish Agency/WZO; the 1962 finding of AZC funding), first degree (AZEC, ZOA, Hadassah), second degree (APC and Christian Council organized by Neumann, the UJA under Montor, the Sonneborn front), third degree (Wagner, Taft, Lodge, Fish, Bloom; Niles, Clifford, Lowenthal, Jacobson; Feinberg, Kaufmann, Golda's tour), and the two flagged loops. Be explicit that a tie is a documented relationship, never shared identity, and that the 1962 finding concerns the AZC, not AZEC. Embed prestate_funding:Overview:0 and prestate_funding:Money:0; figure: power structure of the tiers.

The seven founding narratives checked against the record, each in one tight paragraph with its documented figure (757,182 and 11% in 1922; no general evacuation order; a two-phase war ended at about 2 to 1; the program, pledge and Mandate predating Hitler by 11–37 years; the two-sided civil war before May 1948; about 7% Jewish-owned land in 1947; over a million US contributors in 1948) and a link to the section that proves it. Give equal weight to the opposite myth ('the Rothschilds paid for it all') and say plainly that the same standard corrects both. Embed prestate_funding:People:1 and prestate_funding:Land:1 and discuss their numbers. Figure: comparison table, claim vs record (four columns at most).

The whole play, 1897–1948, step by step, as the chapter's closing synthesis of the pre-state build: bank, land fund, American machine, Balfour, Keren Hayesod, the 1921 tours, Lodge–Fish, the Palestine pound, the enlarged Agency, Christian committees, Haavara, Biltmore, AZEC, the 1944 platforms, the Sonneborn network, Golda's tour, Czech arms and the New York-printed notes; then what this chapter's 1948–1953 sections added on top (armistice lines, absentee law, Law of Return, reparations, bonds). State the finding at its documented size: the Holocaust changed urgency and politics but did not create the apparatus. Embed prestate_funding:The Build:0; maps: state_build and money_1948; this section carries the chapter's synthesis diagram (power structure of the architecture as it stood in 1953).

The +load metaphor as a labeled reading, not a finding: what +load does in Objective-C, the walkthrough, the street version, and what it maps to (Jewish Colonial Trust and Anglo-Palestine Bank 1899–1902, the JNF 1901, Article 4's Jewish agency 1922, AZEC in the 1940s). Mark it clearly as an interpretive device, keep it short, and note the limits of the analogy (no single programmer; contingency and opposition at every step). Map: state_build.
